newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares regain composure after recent slide.
newsitem.headline: German shares regain composure after recent slide.

text.p: German shares continued their recovery on Monday after huge losses registered in the bearish slide of the previous week, with support coming from a firmer opening on Wall Street and a revival in the dollar's fortunes.

The IBIS DAX index ended trade at 3,342.77 points, up 3.32 percent or 107.42 points, after the Dow Jones Industrial index rose 0.61 percent to 6,566.11 points as trade got under way on Wall Street and the dollar settled just above 1.70 marks.
"The sunshine is not only outside today. The dollar is helping and the absence of macroeconomic news from the U.S. is also not a negligible factor," a Frankfurt trader said.
Earlier the DAX index, which tracks bourse trade, ended the day at 3,312.88 point, up 67.95 points or 2.09 percent.
"People are not going wholeheartedly into the recovery -- the volumes are still pretty thin," said Josh Waiblinger of BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Chief among volume leaders over the day was the chemical giant BASF AG, which ended up 4.5 percent at 66.09 marks.
"The BASF analysts' meeting was on Thursday, which was well received, but buying didn't really start until Friday, when people could see what happened with the U.S. data," said Waiblinger.
Other chemicals were also higher, boosted by the dollar. Bayer AG ended electronic trade up 4.4 percent at 69.22 marks while Hoechst AG ended up 3.53 percent at 67.40 marks.
Other strong performers included telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom , closing up 5.39 percent at 37.73 marks, and software group SAP, which ended up 5.19 percent at 284 marks.
After a hectic week or so, many dealers were pleased to see an end to the slide but were unwilling to give anything other than short-term prognoses.
Chartists said that German stock market bulls are down, but not out, and that technicals pointed to the market rising again after the current consolidation period runs its course.

"A key question is whether the gap that we saw last week can be filled and whether the market can break through extremely strong resistance at 3,330 points," said Wieland Staud, chief strategist in German equities at Yamaichi Bank.
"If this decisive point of resistance is broken, then it is likely that the index will rise very quickly to around 3,410 points," Staud said.
"I see the recent fall as an interruption to the bull market, which could last six or eight weeks. But it does not mean the end of the bull market altogether," he said.
